ex: He sprang into the saddle easily as a bird, got the quirt from the horn, and gave his pony a slash with it.
He paused a moment and flicked a sage-brush with his quirt.
[…] when the young man whirled his horse, “hazed” Jupiter in circles and belaboured him with a rawhide quirt, […] He ceased his cavortings […]

s.def: To strike with a quirt.

ety: Named after Norwegian military officer Vidkun Quisling (1887–1945), who ruled the Nazi collaborationist government of Norway during World War Two. From Quislinus, Latinization of Quislin, based on the Danish place name Kvislemark. This term first appeared in 1940. The surname is seemingly supposed to mean "one who is from Kvislemark", and is equivalent to Kvisle(mark) + -ing (suffix designating a person of a certain origin or with certain qualities). However, the earlier form of the name, Quisl…

s.def: A traitor who collaborates with the enemy.
ex: It is time to clear out the quislings and paid flunkies of city hall and big business.

s.def: present participle and gerund of quisle

ety: From Middle English quiten, quyten, from Anglo-Norman quitter, Old French quitter, from quitte (“acquitted, quit”), ultimately from Latin quietus, which itself derives from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyéh₁-ti-s, from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”). Doublet of coy, quite, quiet, and quietus. Compare Dutch kwijten (“to quit”), German Low German quitten (“to quit”), German quitten, quittieren, Danish kvitte, Swedish qvitta, kvitta (“to quit, leave, set off”), Icelandic kvitta.

s.def: To resign from (a job, office, position, etc.).
ex: After having to work overtime without being paid, I quit my job.

s.def: To stop, give up (an activity).
ex: John is planning to quit smoking.

s.def: Released from obligation, penalty, etc; free, clear, or rid.
To leave (a place).
ex: The British quit India in the 1940s.
Jones had no sooner quitted the room, than the petty-fogger, in a whispering tone, asked Mrs Whitefield, “If she knew who that fine spark was?”
... to cause the tenants to quit and give the plaintiff possession of the cottages, &c., ...

s.def: To set at rest; to free, as from anything harmful or oppressive; to relieve; to clear; to liberate.
ex: To quit you […] of this fear, […]you have already lookt Death in the face; what have you found so terrible in it?

s.def: To release from obligation, accusation, penalty, etc.; to absolve; to acquit.
To abandon, renounce (a thing).
To close (an application).
To pay (a debt, fine etc.).
ex: Edmund, enkindle all the sparkes of Nature To quit this horrid acte.
that judge that quits each soul his hire

s.def: To conduct or acquit (oneself); to behave (in a specified way).

ety: From quitch + grass.

s.def: A species of grass, Elymus repens.
ex: Other enemies, like the smaller weeds, he could overcome, but injustice, that quitch grass of life, was what stung him to fury.

ety: From Middle English quiteclaymen, from Anglo-Norman quiteclamer, from clamer quite (“to claim quit”). Compare claim quit.

s.def: To relinquish or release (a claim, title, etc.); to transfer (an interest in property).
A renunciation of claims.
A deed that is a renunciation of claims to a parcel of real property and a transfer of one's claims to another.

s.def: To a moderate extent or degree; somewhat, rather.
ex: Mind your shoes, the basement is quite wet.

s.def: to the greatest extent; completely
To the greatest extent or degree; completely, entirely.
ex: Nobuyoshi Araki has been called a monster, a pornographer and a genius—and the photographer quite agrees.

s.def: In a fully justified sense; truly, perfectly, actually.
ex: "My little plot has been rather successful, after all, hasn't it?" "Quite a perfect success," said Drake.
While the government claims to lead the world with its plans to reduce carbon dioxide emissions, the figures tell quite a different story.

s.def: Indicates agreement; exactly so.
ex: “That's a rather ugly colour for a house, don't you think?” — “Quite.”

s.def: A series of passes made with the cape to distract the bull.

ety: From Middle English quytaunce, from Old French quitance (modern French quittance), from Latin quietantia. The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: A release or acquittal.
A discharge from a debt or obligation; a document that shows this discharge.
ex: I marvel why I answer’d not again; But that’s all one: omittance is no quittance.

s.def: Recompense; return; repayment.
To acquit; to repay.

ety: From Middle English quitter, from Anglo-Norman quiture, quyture et al., specialised use of quiture (“burn mark, burning”), from the participle stem of cuire (“to cook”), or from Latin coctura (“cooking”).

s.def: Matter flowing from a wound or sore; pus.
Alternative spelling of quittor (“fistulous wound at the top of a horse's foot”).
Scoria of tin.
To suppurate; ooze with pus.
One who quits, as:
ex: Winners never quit and quitters never win.
Don't be a quitter — hang in there!
Well, they underestimated Hartlepool, and they underestimated me because I am a fighter and not a quitter!

s.def: A leaver.
A deliverer.

ety: From Middle English quiter, quitere, quitoure, quiture, quytur, whitour, from Old French cuiture, quiture, probably from Latin coctura. Cognate with Low German kwater, kwader (“rottenness”).

s.def: A chronic abscess, or fistula of the coronet, in a horse's foot, resulting from inflammation of the tissues investing the coffin bone.

ety: From Middle English quiver, from Anglo-Norman quivre, from Old Dutch cocare (source of Dutch koker, and cognate to Old English cocer (“quiver, case”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kokar (“container”), said to be from Hunnic, possibly from Proto-Mongolic *kökexür (“leather vessel for liquids”); see there for more. Replaced early modern cocker, the inherited reflex of that West Germanic word. The mathematical sense originated as German Köcher in a 1972 paper by Pierre Gabriel; it was likely chosen…

s.def: A container for arrows, crossbow bolts or darts, such as those fired from a bow, crossbow or blowgun.
ex: Arrows were carried in quiver, called also an arrow case, which served for the magazine, arrows for immediate use were worn in the girdle.

s.def: A ready storage location for figurative tools or weapons.
ex: He's got lots of sales pitches in his quiver.

s.def: A vulva.
The collective noun for cobras.
A multidigraph, especially in the context of representation theory.
Nimble, active.
ex: [...] there was a little quiver fellow, and 'a would manage you his piece thus; and 'a would about and about, and come you in and come you in.

s.def: To shake or move with slight and tremulous motion.
ex: And left the limbs still quivering on the ground.
And the moonlight on the Church seemed to shift and quiver—some pigeons perhaps had been disturbed up there.

s.def: The act of quivering.
ex: I feel a quiver every time we kiss / The sky's the limit with a love like this

ety: Derived from Spanish Quixote, the surname of Don Quixote, the title character in the novel by Miguel de Cervantes, + -ic.

s.def: Resembling or characteristic of the Spanish chivalric hero Don Quixote; possessed with or resulting from the desire to do noble and romantic deeds, without thought of realism and practicality.
ex: Olivier, as you know, was quixotic, and would not permit a secret service and spies.
The message is not subliminal. […] Characters aren’t just quixotic, they cite Cervantes to one another.
In the digital age, building a new library filled with old-fashioned printed books seems idealistic, almost quixotic.

s.def: Overly optimistic and moralistic.
Exceedingly idealistic.
A quixotic person or sentiment.

s.def: A competition in the answering of questions.
ex: We came second in the pub quiz.

s.def: An odd, puzzling or absurd person or thing.
ex: I've always heard he was a quiz, says another, or a quoz, or some such word ; but I did not know he was such a book-worm.
I tell you I am going to the music shop. I trust to your honour. Lord Rawson, I know, will call me a fool for trusting to the honour of a quiz.
Where did you get that quiz of a hat? It makes you look like an old witch.

s.def: One who questions or interrogates; a prying person.
A school examination of less importance, or of greater brevity, than others given in the same course.
To hoax; to chaff or mock with pretended seriousness of discourse; to make sport of, as by obscure questions.
ex: he quizzed unmercifully all the men in the room—

s.def: To peer at; to eye suspiciously or mockingly.
To question (someone) closely, to interrogate.
ex: He quizzed the suspect for around half an hour.

s.def: To instruct (someone) by means of a quiz.
To play with a quiz.

s.def: Questioning or suggesting puzzlement.
ex: Miss Moneypenny would have been desirable but for eyes which were cool and direct and quizzical.
But I did see things that aren't yet quite right, and at which I raised a quizzical eyebrow.

s.def: Strange or eccentric.
Jocose; humorous.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic الْقُنَيْطِرَة (al-qunayṭira). Doublet of Kenitra.

s.def: A city in the Quneitra governorate, Syria
A governorate of Syria

ety: Abbreviation of quadrangle; originally (17th century) referring to the quadrangles of Newgate Prison, London.

s.def: A quadrangle or court, as of a prison; a prison.
ex: […]and declined their escort, desiring to be conducted to “quod” by the gallant South Australian police,[…].
Pity McNamara′s still doing his stretch in the quod, but he′ll be out soon.

s.def: Confinement in a prison.
To confine in prison.
Quoth.
ex: “Why,” quod her friend, “would ye not willingly have gone with your company, if God should so have suffered it?”
“And therefore I have granted to their request,” quod the King;[…].

ety: Variant of coin; compare coign.

s.def: Any of the corner building blocks of a building, usually larger or more ornate than the surrounding blocks.
The keystone of an arch.
A metal wedge which fits into the space between the type and the edge of a chase, and is tightened to fix the metal type in place.
ex: Next fit the quoins, using the “persuader” to squeeze in the pages, and tap up all around.

s.def: A form of wedge used to prevent casks from moving.
A wedge of wood or iron put under the breech of heavy guns or the muzzle of siege-mortars to raise them to the proper level.
A number of apple varieties with a distinctive ribbed appearance, like corners of a coin.
To wedge or steady with quoins.

ety: From Middle English coyte (“flat stone”), from Old French coite, from Latin culcita. Doublet of quilt.

s.def: A flat disc of metal or stone thrown at a target in the game of quoits.
ex: He heard then a warm heavy sigh, softer, as she turned over and the loose brass quoits of the bedstead jingled. Must get those settled really.

s.def: A ring of rubber or rope similarly used in the game of deck-quoits.
The flat stone covering a cromlech.
ex: This quoit was brought from a karn about a furlong distance, near which is another cromlech, not so large.

s.def: An ancient burial mound, synonymous with dolmen.
The discus used in ancient sports.
To play quoits.
To throw like a quoit.

ety: From Nyunga kwaka.

s.def: A cat-sized wallaby, Setonix brachyurus, of southwestern Australia.

ety: Borrowed from Latin quondam. Compare whilom.

s.def: Former; once; at one time.
ex: However, with the dainty volume my quondam friend sprang into fame. At the same time he cast off the chrysalis of a commonplace existence.
For the sleeper on the couch was not Akeley at all, but my quondam guide Noyes.

ety: Inherited from Middle English quorum (c. 1426), from Anglo-Norman quorum, clipped from the Anglo-Latin wording of commissions in which certain persons were specially designated as members of a body by the words quorum vos unum esse volumus ad etc. (“of whom we want you to be one assigned to etc.”). Latin quōrum is the masculine genitive plural of the relative pronoun quī (“who”).

s.def: minimum number present for official business
Distinguished or essential members of any body; a select company.
The minimum number of votes that a distributed transaction has to obtain in order to be allowed to perform an operation in a distributed system.

A select body of (usually eminent) justices of the peace, every member of which had to be present to constitute a deciding body; a member of this body. Later more generally: all justices collectively.
The minimum number of members required for a group to officially conduct business and to cast votes, often but not necessarily a majority or supermajority.
ex: We can discuss the issue tonight but cannot vote until we have a quorum.

ety: From Latin quota pars; see Latin quota.

s.def: A proportional part or share; the share or proportion assigned to each in a division.
A prescribed number or percentage that may serve as, for example, a maximum, a minimum, or a goal.
A restriction on the import of something to a specific quantity.

s.def: A price that has been quoted for buying or selling.
ex: Let's get a quotation for repairing the roof before we decide whether it's worth doing.

s.def: A fragment of a human expression that is repeated by somebody else, for example from literature or a famous speech.
ex: "Where they burn books, they will also burn people" is a famous quotation from Heinrich Heine.

s.def: The act of quoting someone or something.
The act of setting a price.
A quota, a share.
plural of quotation mark

s.def: A statement attributed to a person; a quotation.
ex: She loved reading quotes of famous people.

s.def: A quotation mark.
A summary of work to be done with a set price; a quotation.
ex: After going over the hefty quotes, the board decided it was cheaper to have the project executed by its own staff.

s.def: A price set and offered (by the potential seller) for a financial security or commodity; a quotation.
To prepare a summary of work to be done and set a price; to estimate.
ex: Can you believe they quoted me $5,000?

s.def: To name the current price, notably of a financial security.
To indicate verbally or by equivalent means the start of a quotation.
To observe, to take account of.
ex: But must our moderne Critticks envious eye Seeme thus to quote some grosse deformity?
I prethe doe, twill be a sceane of mirth For me to quote his passions and his smiles, His amorous haviour, …

s.def: To repeat (the exact words of a person).
ex: The writer quoted the president's speech.

s.def: Used in speech to indicate the start of a quotation.
ex: She told me she was, quote, "too hot for you."

ety: From Middle English quoth, quath, from Old English cwæþ (first and third person past indicative of cweþan (“to say, speak to, address, exhort, admonish”)), from Proto-Germanic *kwaþ (first and third person past indicative of Proto-Germanic *kweþaną (“to say”)). Unrelated to quote.

s.def: Said.
ex: “Pull, if ye never pull’d before; / Good ringers, pull your best,” quoth he.

s.def: To say.
ex: The old cow laughs, for she feels sure of a square dear now; and the wise riven quoths; quoths he: “Tis well done, let the good work go on,”[…]
“’Ods blood!” quoths Lee, “’Tis ‘Honey Dew.’”
Gunn-ar quoths to Eve: “Hail dawn![…]”

ety: From Anglo-Norman cotidian, cotidien, Middle French cotidian, cotidien, and their source, Latin cottīdiānus, quōtīdiānus (“happening every day”), from adverb cottīdiē, quōtīdiē (“every day, daily”), from an unattested adjective derived from quot (“how many”) + locative form of diēs (“day”).

s.def: Happening every day; daily.
Having the characteristics of something which can be seen, experienced, etc, every day or very commonly.
ex: The story or the painting would serve to connect the part with the whole, the event with the myth, the quotidian with the sacred.
Tragedy demanded verse, not the quotidian prose of comedy, and verse usually supplied some form of end rhyme.
Grids are used for such quotidian items as stationery, business cards, mailing labels, hang tags, instruction manuals, etc.

s.def: Recurring every twenty-four hours or (more generally) daily (of symptoms, etc).
ex: Quotidian periodicity we find in greater or less degree in nearly all fevers, particularly in fevers associated with suppuration.
I regret that the effect of these statements is a denial of the observation of initial quotidian paroxysms following artificial inoculation.

s.def: Something which is considered humdrum or dull.
ex: His life took on a quotidian humdrum.

s.def: A fever which recurs every day; quotidian malaria.
ex: If I could meet that Fancie-monger, I would giue him some good counsel, for he seemes to haue the Quotidian of Loue vpon him.

s.def: A daily allowance formerly paid to certain members of the clergy.
Commonplace or mundane things regarded as a class.

ety: Borrowed from Latin quotiēns, from quotiēs.

s.def: The number (either a fraction or an integer) resulting from the division of one number by another.
ex: Dividing 12 by 4 yields a quotient of 3.

s.def: By analogy, the result of any process that is the inverse of multiplication as defined for any mathematical entities other than numbers.
A quotum or quota.
The number of runs scored per wicket lost when batting, divided by the number of runs conceded per wicket taken when bowling — used as a league table tiebreaker in some first-class tournaments.
A mathematical structure formed by identifying elements within a larger one.
To identify elements within a mathematical structure so as to create a quotient.
ex: We show that such deformations still exists after quotienting out by diffeomorphisms only if the non linear addition is non associative.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic الْقُرْآن (al-qurʔān), definite form of قُرْآن (qurʔān, “act of reciting”), verbal noun of قَرَأَ (qaraʔa, “to recite; to read (aloud)”). (The obsolete alternative spellings with "al-", like the Alcoran, redundantly retained the Arabic definite article.) Compare Classical Syriac ܩܪܝܢܐ (qeryānā, “reading; scripture”).

s.def: The Islamic holy book, considered by Muslims to be the word of God as revealed to Muhammad.

ety: From Quran + -ism.

s.def: A denomination in Islam that generally rejects the authoritative role of hadiths, and considers the Qur'an to be the only dependable religious text.

ety: From Quran + -ist.

s.def: An adherent of the Ahle Quran branch of Islam.

ety: From Qutb + -ism.

s.def: An Islamist ideology developed by Sayyid Qutb, the figurehead of the Muslim Brotherhood, involving the use of military force to propagate sharia law.
ex: The ideology of Qutbism was pursued by Muhammad Abdul al-Salam Faraj, who emerged after Qutb as Egypt's most important Islamist revolutionaries.

ety: From Qutb + -ist.

s.def: Of or pertaining to Qutbism.
A supporter of Qutbism.
